reason: The verb h₂idnéwti means 'swell', not 'come', so 'Will he come here?' is mistranslated; the verb for 'come' is gʷémt, as used in the next sentence.
'with us' needs the comitative case (instrumental or accusative after ḱóm), but n̥sméy is dative, which ḱóm does not govern.
'wédnōm' is a genitive plural, but 'the water' is the direct object of 'carry' and needs the accusative singular (wódr̥), as the later 'wódr̥' correctly uses.
The English question 'Did he devour the goat?' needs a third-person verb, but gʷr̥h₃éte is a second-person plural form (-te), not a 3SG form like the later gʷr̥h₃ét.
The question 'Did you fight over the spring?' needs a form of the verb 'fight', but h₁wogʷʰéyes is analysed as 'vow', a different verb.
The adjective 'other' is a dual form, but it modifies the singular ablative noun ḱóymōd 'village' and must agree in number and case.
The English says 'no wolf came', but the PIE has no negation (no ne or ne-type particle) before h₁ludʰét, so the negation is lost.
The address 'sister-in-law' needs a vocative, but ǵl̥h₂éwi is parsed as locative singular, which is the wrong case for the role.
The object 'the pot' is rendered by bʰléh₁wom, which the analysis gives as the adjective 'colorful' (ACC.SG), not a noun for pot, so the sentence has no correct object for 'hide the pot'.
'to the old man' needs a masculine accusative after próti 'towards', but this is a feminine locative singular form.
The opening vocative 'stéla' means 'earth mound', not 'grandmother' (which is h₂énHe, used later in the text).

Each clause matches the English: vocative, middle past 'was born', imperative 'set', genitive/dative pronouns, aorist 'died', subjunctives for the future and modal forms, and the neuter accusative adjective agreeing with h₁nómn̥.
The English question 'Do they not eat the wheat?' is negative, but the PIE question 'puHróm gʷr̥h₃ónti?' has no negation particle, so the negation is lost.
The English says the speaker presently grasps ('I grasp it'), but h₁épm̥ is an aorist or past 1SG form, so the tense is wrong; the present would be needed.
The English says 'by the fire', but h₃n̥gʷéni is the locative of h₃éngʷn̥ 'fat', so the noun has the wrong meaning.
The English 'It does not love her' has its negation dropped: the PIE 'h₁íh₂m̥ lubʰyéti h₁íd dʰréwgʰt' lacks a 'ne', so the negation is missing.
The English 'on the earth' needs the word for earth (dʰéǵʰōm, locative dʰéǵʰmi), but donḱéh₂ is glossed as 'tongs'.

'Wealth' is singular in the English ('Wealth feeds a house', with a singular verb), but this form is parsed as dual, not the singular h₃épnos; the h₁éterōy 'to the other' in the horses clause also reverses the English 'the one has many horses'.
The English says the wind 'does not shake' the post, but the PIE has no negative particle (such as ne or mḗ) before the verb, so the negation is lost.
The English says 'Men hide nothing', but the PIE 'h₂néres kʷid ḱélonti' has no negation, so 'kʷid' (an interrogative 'what/anything') leaves the negation out and reads as 'Men hide something'.
The English says the wife 'was not giving' food, but the PIE has no negation (no ne or mḗ) before dédeh₃t, so the negation is lost.
The English 'You owe me nothing' needs a negation (e.g. ne/nēd + kʷid), but the PIE 'moy kʷid dʰl̥gʰési' has none, so it reads as 'you owe me something'.
The reflexive ablative swṓd ('from my field') agrees with h₂éǵros, which the analysis reads only as NOM.SG, so the noun's case does not match the ablative the sentence needs.
The English says 'will not sleep here', but the PIE sentence 'pótnih₂ moy h₁idʰé séseti' has no negation (ne is missing before séseti).

The English asks 'Where is the ford?' with no possessive, but h₁swós means 'your' (plural), adding an unsupported word, and the sentence has no 'is' verb to match its analysed PRS.1DU reading.
pnéwmn̥ means 'breath/spirit', not 'cattle', so the object of 'drive the cattle out' is mistranslated (the cattle would need a word like pḱú or gʷṓws).
The English says 'I shall pour it', but the engine glosses h₂téwǵoh₂ as the verb 'spread terror', so the verb means the wrong thing.
The English says "I am not sad", but the PIE "h₁eǵóh₂ luǵréh₂" has no negation (no ne), so it asserts the opposite.

The English says 'in a stone' (singular, locative), but the PIE form h₂éḱmonh₁e is a dual (nominative/accusative/vocative) rather than a singular locative.
